subject: Communication
title: Source Evaluation: The SIFT Method
description: A micro-lesson that makes Source Evaluation: The SIFT Method usable.

hook.text: A professional-looking website claims a miracle cure. Before you believe it, SIFT: Stop, Investigate, Find, Trace.

buildup.text: Mike Caulfield's SIFT method: Stop (pause before sharing), Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace claims.

discovery.text: Most misinformation succeeds because people react before investigating. Emotion moves faster than verification.

twist.text: Website design and professional appearance have zero correlation with accuracy. The most polished sites can be the least truthful.

climax.text: SIFT takes less than 60 seconds and catches most misinformation. A tiny habit that makes you dramatically harder to deceive.

punchline.text: Before you share, SIFT. Sixty seconds can save you from spreading a lie.

details.summary: The SIFT method provides a simple framework for evaluating online information: Stop before sharing, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, and Trace claims to their origin. Created by Mike Caulfield, SIFT takes seconds and dramatically improves information evaluation.
details.whyItMatters: SIFT gives you a practical, fast method for evaluating information quality before it shapes your beliefs or gets shared further.
takeaways: SIFT: Stop, Investigate, Find better coverage, Trace claims
It takes seconds and integrates into daily browsing habits
Created by digital literacy expert Mike Caulfield

faq.question: How does SIFT differ from traditional source evaluation?
faq.answer: Traditional methods like the CRAAP test ask you to analyze a source deeply. SIFT prioritizes speed: Stop your emotional reaction, quickly check the source's reputation, find the same story from trusted outlets, and trace surprising claims to their origin. It matches the pace of online browsing.

faq.question: What does tracing claims to the origin actually involve?
faq.answer: When a claim cites a study or statistic, find the original source. Often claims become distorted through repeated sharing. A study saying X might correlate with Y becomes X causes Y in a headline. Finding the primary source reveals whether the claim accurately represents the evidence.
